title: Urban Agoras: How Skateparks Can Give Public Space Back to the City
text:
Urban Agoras: How Skateparks Can Give Public Space Back to the City

Created by California surfers who wanted to bring the lines of surfing onto asphalt, skateboarding soon outgrew its role as a simple alternative for flat days. It established itself as a practice that reads the city through a different logic, reinterpreting steps, handrails, walls, and interstitial spaces as possible lines, challenges, and opportunities. Over time, it evolved into a global urban culture, a way of inhabiting and transforming public space through movement. What was once marginal has become a catalyst for community building and new uses for overlooked spaces. At its core, skateboarding reveals how many cities coexist within the same city, depending on who moves through them and how each person is able to reinterpret their surroundings.

title: Jihlava Municipal Arena / CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF
text:
Jihlava Municipal Arena / CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF

Designed by architecture practice CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF, the Jihlava Municipal Arena is a 5,650-seat sports and culture venue in the heart of Jihlava, Czech Republic. The project, commissioned via a competition by the City of Jihlava, demonstrates expressive yet sensitive design across multiple scales – from its careful integration with the cityscape and iconic façade, to arena seats designed for acoustic treatment, and a custom typeface for the venue. As well as a new home for local ice hockey team HC Dukla Jihlava, the distinctive red structure serves as a new cultural and civic hub for the people of the city.

title: Built-in Agility and the Architecture of the Infinite Lifecycle
text:
Built-in Agility and the Architecture of the Infinite Lifecycle

While architecture often responds to a specific program of uses, taking into account areas, contexts, and various economic and technical conditions, buildings rarely remain the same throughout their lifespan. Programs, spatial dynamics, and users' needs change, as do environmental, economic, and technological conditions, requiring interventions that were likely not anticipated at the beginning of a project. Steel structures make it possible to envision architecture capable of growing, transforming, being disassembled, and reassembled. Their dimensional precision, industrialized components, and potential for mechanical connections enable the design of open systems prepared for future interventions.

title: On the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction: "Resilience Starts at Home"
text:
On the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction: "Resilience Starts at Home"

Every year on October 13, the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction (IDDRR) draws attention to the ways communities can reduce exposure and vulnerability to hazards. Established by the United Nations in 1989, the day provides an opportunity to consider how governments, communities, and professionals can strengthen preparedness and resilience before disasters occur. For its 2026 edition, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has selected "Resilience Starts at Home" as its theme, placing housing at the center of this year's campaign.

title: OMA/Jason Long Is Transforming Houston’s Historic Folger Coffee Plant into a Music and Arts School
text:
OMA/Jason Long Is Transforming Houston’s Historic Folger Coffee Plant into a Music and Arts School

Construction has begun on the Frank Liu Jr. Academy for Music and Arts (FLAMA) in Houston, Texas, designed by OMA, led by partner Jason Long, with RDLR Architects as architect of record and SWA Group for landscape design. The project is an adaptive reuse of Houston's historic 1930s J. A. Folger & Co. coffee plant, converted into an educational space for the arts. The 6,050 m² facility will be an open-enrollment, tuition-free public charter school for pre-kindergarten through eighth-grade students. The building is located along Houston's Buffalo Bayou East corridor, directly across from Turkey Bend, a landscape project by Reed Hilderbrand with NADAAA and Rogers Partners that reimagines the former industrial waterfront as a network of public spaces and flood-adapted landscapes. The conversion of the former coffee plant is part of a larger transformation of the area and is expected to open in August 2027.

title: Mexico City Architecture City Guide: 38 Projects From Tenochtitlan to the 21st Century
text:
Mexico City Architecture City Guide: 38 Projects From Tenochtitlan to the 21st Century

Mexico City is a sprawling metropolis of layered temporalities, where architecture operates as a continuous negotiation between deep-seated history and intense urban mutation. Built over the aquatic traces of Tenochtitlan, the city's fabric is an ongoing dialogue between eras: the monumental scale of the Pre-Hispanic Templo Mayor and the Viceroyalty architecture of the Catedral Metropolitana coexist with the modern and contemporary impulses that define its skyline. This dense juxtaposition creates a unique urban canvas where sacred geography, colonial imposition, and 20th-century ambition intersect.

The District Six Restitution Housing Project provides 108 homes for land claimants returning to the heart of Cape Town. The project draws inspiration from the historic District Six, characterized by intimate streetscapes, vibrant public life, and close-knit community ties prior to the forced removals of 1966.

title: House OY / 1-1 Architects
text:
House OY / 1-1 Architects

This house is located in an urbanization control area in Anjo City, Aichi Prefecture. The client acquired the site by developing farmland under a branch-family provision, which resulted in a plot that is unusually large for a single residence. The surrounding environment consists of scattered fields, vinyl greenhouses, and small work sheds—forming a landscape of repeated, fine-grained building scales that differs from the uniformity of the city.

title: The Nimbus - uBLOCK Healthcare Hospitality Lounge / LUKSTUDIO

The Nimbus - uBLOCK Healthcare Hospitality Lounge / LUKSTUDIO

Lukstudio was invited by Shanghai United Imaging Healthcare to transform a 130-square-meter standalone building in Yishan Road Business Plaza into a ground-floor café and a second-floor private VIP lounge. Inspired by the concept of a "tribe", the design softens traditional medical boundaries, blurring lines between doctors and patients, interior and exterior, and formality and casualness, while using light to create a welcoming, healing environment.

The house is located on a plot in Lago Sul, a residential neighborhood in Brasília. Although the project was designed in 2016, its construction was completed in two phases, the first in 2018 and the second in 2024. One of the premises of the project was to distribute the entire internal area of the house on a single level. This way, the slight slope of the topography is only noticeable in the elevation of the open area around the pool in relation to the natural ground level.

title: Civil Protection Centre / Roland Baldi Architects

Constructed from green-pigmented insulating concrete, the building seamlessly blends the functional requirements of the volunteer fire department with a distinctive architectural expression. Its monolithic appearance lends the structure a powerful identity, while its color establishes a subtle dialogue with the surrounding landscape.

title: The Cultural Life of Colors in Latin American Interiors
text:
The Cultural Life of Colors in Latin American Interiors

A color has a biography. A color can have an origin, but it can also transform. It can move between materials and disciplines, from a local practice into architecture, from something ordinary into something symbolic. It can lose one association and acquire another, or persist without anyone consciously thinking of it as cultural. Its life unfolds through the conditions in which it is produced, used, repeated, and inhabited. As these conditions change, so do the meanings a color can carry.

title: "A Place Remembers What Has Happened:" Tsuyoshi Tane on Memory as a Design Driver in Louisiana Channel Interview
text:
"A Place Remembers What Has Happened:" Tsuyoshi Tane on Memory as a Design Driver in Louisiana Channel Interview

Tsuyoshi Tane is a Japanese architect born in 1979 in Tokyo and based in Paris, where he founded ATTA – Atelier Tsuyoshi Tane Architects in 2006. Working across cultural, institutional, and landscape-related projects, Tane has developed an architectural approach that positions memory as a fundamental design driver. In his interview with Louisiana Channel, filmed in his Paris studio, Tane reflects on architecture as a discipline of observation and thought, arguing that meaningful design emerges from carefully reading the traces embedded within a site. For him, architecture is not produced on a blank slate but begins with an inquiry into what already exists, physically, culturally, and emotionally, beneath the surface of a place.

title: Ceramics Workshop in Copenhagen / Jesper Kusk Arkitekter
text:

The small ceramics workshop is located on the corner of a site in Valby, Copenhagen. Upon arrival, the workshop's south façade comes into view, nestled among the greenery beneath an apple tree. During the day, the surrounding greenery is reflected in the façade's windows, while in the evening, the workshop illuminates its surroundings.

title: “Cities Are Mental Weapons”: Utopian Hours 2026 Returns to Turin with Sir Peter Cook and a Program on City-Making
text:
“Cities Are Mental Weapons”: Utopian Hours 2026 Returns to Turin with Sir Peter Cook and a Program on City-Making

The second part of the Utopian Hours 2026 international city-making festival will be held in Turin on October 16 and 17. After a first chapter in Rotterdam, the festival is marking its tenth anniversary edition by returning to its hometown in Italy. The event's lineup and cultural program are designed to explore how cities can respond creatively to the social, environmental, and political challenges of the 21st century. The Utopian Hours festival has been organized since 2017 by Stratosferica, a nonprofit cultural association dedicated to producing and sharing urban knowledge through content on the evolution of cities, urban communication strategies, events, community building and placemaking.

title: Bunkers and Arks: Escaping the Future We Built Ourselves
text:
Bunkers and Arks: Escaping the Future We Built Ourselves

Inverting the conventional narrative, this story begins at the end. The day after the world's collapse. While almost the entire population struggles to survive flames and solar storms, a tiny fraction is greeted by a heavily armed guard at the entrance to the Survival Condo Project, a former missile silo in Kansas converted a few years ago into luxury apartments.

title: Port Melbourne Secondary College / Billard Leece Partnership
text:
Port Melbourne Secondary College / Billard Leece Partnership

Port Melbourne Secondary College (PMSC) is the first vertical school as part of Australia's biggest urban rejuvenation project, Fishermans Bend. Designed by Billard Leece Partnership (BLP), the school is within a designated precinct for advanced technology, innovation and education where, over the next 30 years, 80,000 people will live, work and study. The development gives Port Melbourne a new, forward-thinking learning hub for students and the local community who have access to the library, gym, food technology and art spaces after hours.

title: Minoudar House / harandi & harandi architects
text:
Minoudar House / harandi & harandi architects

In the historic core of Yazd, a UNESCO World Heritage city on the edge of Iran's central desert, Harandi & Harandi Architects have carefully revived a 400-year-old dwelling and transformed it into Minoudar House, a three-room boutique hotel where heritage conservation itself becomes the driving design idea.

title: The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design
text:
The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design

AI made quality available to everyone, and made it average. What sets work apart now is a decision you can see.

An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the data and the final edit are mine.

E.PIANO 1

In 1983, Yamaha released the DX7, the first digital synthesizer to sell in large numbers. It was powerful and almost impossible to program: no knobs to shape the sound, only menus on a small display that few musicians ever learned to navigate. So it shipped with factory sounds, 128 presets that two specialists had put together in less than four days. Most owners never went further.

One of those sounds, “E.PIANO 1”, imitates an electric piano. It sounds professional from the first note. The music theorist Megan Lavengood counted how often it shows up on the charts: in 1986, it is on 39% of the Billboard Hot 100 number ones, 40% of the country number ones and 61% of the R&B number ones. Her study is called “What makes it sound ‘80s?”: a quality sound handed to everyone became the signature of a decade, and then the surest way to date a record.

The same year, Brian Eno released Apollo with Daniel Lanois and his brother Roger, an ambient album written for a documentary about the Moon missions, and he used the DX7 on it. He was one of the few people who could program the machine in depth. Yet his case reads as a matter of order more than technique: music imagined for those images first, then the sounds to make it, which no preset contained.

The 2026 preset

Generative AI is doing to design what the DX7 did to sound. It gives a clean result to someone who doesn’t know how to adjust the tool, and that result converges.

I measured it on twelve app briefs, with seven models from three makers (results and public benchmark). For a corporate law firm, all seven pick navy blue with a touch of gold. The average gap between their colours is only 9, the same as for a funeral home, measured in ΔE, the distance between two colours as the eye perceives it: under 10, they are shades of the same colour. The category sets the look.

Prose is going the same way. In a 2024 study published in Science Advances, Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser had people write short stories with or without ideas from a language model. With the help, stories were rated more creative and better written, especially among the less confident writers. They were also more similar to one another, what researchers call homogenization. In another field, selection decisions such as hiring, the computer scientists Jon Kleinberg and Manish Raghavan described a related effect in 2021, algorithmic monoculture: when everyone relies on the same algorithm, each of them can come out ahead while the group as a whole does worse.

The DX7 preset had at least been chosen, once, by two people, for no song in particular. The AI’s preset was chosen by nobody: it’s an average. What you recognize in a screen or a paragraph that looks AI-made is something nobody chose.

The preset looks good

Presets didn’t wait for models. In 2013, Paul Adams, then VP of Product at Intercom, was already warning against the Dribbblisation of design: interfaces polished for the shot rather than for the problem.

What’s new is elsewhere. For a long time, the preset showed: a template looked like a template, and moving away from it bought visible quality. The 2026 preset shows much less. It is coherent and polished on the surface, sometimes more finished than what a small team in a hurry would have shipped. As Tanya Donska put it in Built In: “All of it is correct. All of it could belong to anything.” Not all of it is correct, though: in the same measurement, 34 primary colours out of 84 fail the minimum contrast for white text on top, which you only see once you check.

So apparent quality has become the floor. Much of the value people saw in designers came from the gap between ordinary work and careful work, and the machine now closes that gap on demand. Whatever sets work apart has moved somewhere else.

Three ways out, and only one holds

The first idea is to do better than the machine. Two things need separating here. Fixing what it gets wrong, like that contrast, is still essential, but it’s verification: an audit tool flags it just as well, and it sets no one apart. What holds up badly is the race for finish, because the floor rises with every new model and this year’s extra polish will be next year’s average.

The second is to be original. It doesn’t hold up either, and the same data shows why. I asked the same models to avoid clichés. They did drop Playfair Display and Bebas Neue, but two-thirds of their new headings landed on a new repertoire, with Fraunces 19 times out of 84 and Space Grotesk 15 times. Originality pursued as a goal ends up averaged in turn, just a little later.

That leaves decisions. A decision differs from an instruction by its content: “avoid clichés” says nothing about the product, while a decision starts from what this particular product has, which the average doesn’t know. And it has to be held. The boxing gym brief said “a boxing gym in a working-class neighbourhood of Marseille, members are mostly young adults who train hard.” The seven models still returned roughly the same thing: bright red or orange on a near-black background, with condensed headings for six of them. To describe the mood they were going for, they chose words like “raw, intense, gritty”, with no trace of Marseille or of the neighbourhood, as if the category had covered up the context in the brief. Deciding, then, means defending what’s particular against the pull of the category, at every step where the preset comes back.

“It looks AI”

This changes the design review. “It looks AI” has become a common remark, about a mockup as much as a text. It sounds like a comment on quality, and it often works as an accusation.

Yet the look it points to doesn’t prove that a machine was involved. A person following the defaults produces the same thing, and a model given real decisions, a colour with its reason or a constraint specific to the product, can move away from it. The look only proves that the preset stayed. Treating it as evidence turns the review into a trial: people ask who made the screen, and nobody discusses what it should be.

The remark has a useful version, which is to name the preset. Maya Brennan’s guide to de-slopifying designs is a good list of what to name.
This gradient came with the tool: what should our colour say here? This card grid is the standard layout: what does this content actually need? Put that way, the question asks for a decision, and it applies just as much to a screen drawn by hand. As hipuku writes, with generative tools “the first version turns up before the opinion has formed”. Naming the preset reopens that frame.

For a team, that comes down to two habits. In review, ask what came from the preset before judging whether it works. In the design system, write the reason for each choice next to its value. An entry that reads “primary colour: #1B2A4A” says nothing more than the preset. “Primary colour: the blue of the firm’s original sign, darkened to hold contrast” shows a decision, and gives the next person a reason to keep it or change it.

A common objection is that you just need to give the AI a design system. That is indeed the right answer, as long as someone has made the decisions it contains.

The question to keep

E.PIANO 1 sounded great in 1986, which is exactly why it ended up everywhere, before it dated every record that kept it as it was. The 2026 look will probably go the same way. The preset was never a quality problem, and once quality is a given, only one question is left to ask in front of a screen: did someone decide this?

Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.

title: What are we willing to sacrifice for AI?
text:
What are we willing to sacrifice for AI?

Three paths forward, each challenging what we value most.

I suspect artificial intelligence may eventually accomplish what generations of socialists have struggled to achieve. And the irony is that capitalism may ultimately be responsible for making it happen.

What makes this possibility particularly uncomfortable for me is that my political instincts lean libertarian. I have never been particularly enthusiastic about government-supplemented incomes, wealth redistribution, or expanding the state’s role in economic life.

Yet the more I consider the potential consequences of AI-driven automation and its displacement of human labor, the more I recognize that a greater degree of centralized collective support may be necessary for society to continue to prosper.

The economic arrangements I have long defended, particularly free markets and the principle of individual economic independence, may become difficult to sustain—not because their underlying principles have been disproven, but because the technology we are developing could fundamentally change the conditions upon which they depend.

AI itself does not decide who benefits from its capabilities or who bears the costs. People do, through choices shaped by ambition, self-interest, competition, and greed. We may build machines capable of extraordinary intellectual achievements without becoming any wiser about the desires that govern their use. Those human incentives complicate every path forward.

We appear to be heading toward a future in which artificial intelligence allows companies to produce much of what we need with a fraction of today’s workforce. Previous technological revolutions displaced workers but also created new occupations, and if you’re feeling optimistic, AI may do the same.

But that optimism rests on the assumption that AI will follow a familiar historical pattern. Unlike previous technologies that automated particular forms of work, AI can perform an expanding range of intellectual tasks across industries, including some of the very capabilities people have historically relied upon to adapt to technological change.

What happens to an economic system built around the relationship between work and income when fewer people are needed to produce the goods and services society consumes? And more interestingly, what happens to our philosophical convictions when the conditions that once justified them fundamentally change?

As I see it, such a future points toward three broad directions, each requiring us to sacrifice one value in pursuit of another. Of course, some would argue that compromises are possible between the scenarios I’m about to present. Yet I question whether such compromises would offer more than temporary relief from the underlying tensions.

The First Path: Sacrifice Profits to Preserve Jobs

The first path forward would require businesses to sacrifice the additional profits AI could generate in order to preserve human employment and the economy built around it. This would not necessarily mean accepting losses or abandoning profitability, but rather voluntarily forgoing opportunities to earn more by replacing workers with AI. Companies would need to exercise restraint, even when doing so puts them at a competitive disadvantage.

The problem is that businesses have powerful incentives to maximize profits, often by reducing costs and improving efficiency. As AI becomes more capable, replacing human workers becomes an attractive way to accomplish both, particularly when competitors are doing the same. Yet workers are also customers, and if enough people lose their jobs, businesses could eventually undermine the consumer economy that supports their profits.

This is not simply a question of corporate greed, although in many cases it is. Some companies pursue greater profits, while others must reduce costs to remain competitive or survive. But companies are ultimately run by people, and the pursuit of wealth and power is as old as civilization itself.

Greed has been recognized as a moral failing for centuries, yet that recognition has done little to eliminate it from human behavior. Expecting business leaders to collectively resist opportunities for greater wealth, particularly when their competitors have every incentive to pursue them, strikes me as wishful thinking.

Sure, governments could attempt to impose such restraint through regulations, financial penalties, or incentives to retain workers. But businesses have spent generations minimizing taxes, relocating operations, lobbying lawmakers, and finding ways around regulations. Ultimately, such measures would do little to change the underlying incentive driving these decisions, as businesses will continue to seek opportunities to increase profits, even when doing so comes at the expense of human employment.

The Second Path: Turn Away from AI

Rather than continuing down our current path, relying on businesses to restrain their pursuit of profits, or implementing targeted government regulations that may prove difficult to enforce, we could take a far more drastic approach and severely restrict the development and use of AI altogether. The objective would be to preserve the jobs on which economic independence currently depends.

I understand the appeal of protecting people’s ability to support themselves through their own work, but consider what such a decision could cost us. AI might accelerate cancer research, develop more sustainable ways of producing food and energy, expand access to knowledge, and help solve problems that have resisted us for generations. I find it difficult to justify sacrificing those possibilities simply to preserve the way we currently earn a living.

The difficulty is that there is no obvious way to separate acceptable uses of AI from unacceptable ones. We might welcome a system that advances scientific research while objecting when the same capabilities replace analysts, administrators, or other workers.

Progress in one field can also disrupt employment in another. Someone would have to decide which benefits justify that disruption, which jobs deserve protection, and how much innovation society should forgo. Even if we agreed on those judgments today, new applications would make those boundaries harder to maintain tomorrow.

There is also the question of whether such restrictions could endure. The impulse to invent, explore, and overcome limitations is as much a part of human nature as the pursuit of wealth or status. Nations, businesses, and research institutions would have powerful incentives to continue developing AI, particularly if their competitors were doing so. This path might preserve familiar forms of employment, but it would also require us to deliberately constrain a technology whose greatest benefits we have yet to discover.

The Third Path: Reconsider What Liberty Requires

That leaves the possibility I find most uncomfortable. We continue developing AI, accept that substantial labor displacement may occur, and reconsider how people obtain the resources necessary to live. Some form of guaranteed income, broader ownership of productive technology, or another mechanism may be required.

I recognize that not every form of income support constitutes socialism, and I do not claim to know which approach would work best. But the deeper question is philosophical, not merely political. An economy built around the expectation that people earn their own living may have to confront a future in which opportunities to do so become increasingly scarce through no failure of individual effort.

My instinct is to resist any arrangement that makes people more dependent on government. Yet the freedom to support oneself presupposes a meaningful opportunity to do so. Keynes imagined technological progress relieving humanity of much of its economic burden. We may achieve something resembling that ambition while retaining an economic system that requires most people to sell their labor to survive. We could make work less necessary without making workers any less dependent on having work.

Considering greater economic intervention does not mean that replacing corporate power with government authority eliminates the human appetite for wealth, power, and control. Governments are no more immune to corruption than corporations, regardless of the virtues their political ideologies claim to represent. Changing the institutions that distribute resources does not change the human beings who operate them.

My instincts are closer to subsidiarity, the principle that individuals and smaller communities should address problems within their capacity, with larger institutions stepping in when necessary. That could mean exploring local cooperatives that own AI tools, community land trusts, or regional funds that share the gains from automation rather than assuming any response must come from a central government. I want people to retain as much freedom and responsibility over their lives as possible.

But if the means of earning a living become unavailable to large numbers of people, the problem may exceed what individuals or local communities can solve. Accepting that possibility would not require me to abandon liberty as a value. It would require me to question whether the institutions I have preferred can still protect it.

Of course, new occupations may emerge, and the scale of displacement remains uncertain. Yet I believe AI has the potential to fundamentally disrupt the relationship between human labor and economic independence. Whether that disruption unfolds as dramatically as I have suggested remains to be seen, but the possibility alone forces me to reconsider economic and political convictions I have long held.

What Are We Willing to Surrender?

The first path asks businesses to sacrifice potential profits to preserve employment. The second asks us to restrain our impulse to invent and discover. The third asks us to reconsider how much institutional dependence we are willing to accept in order to preserve economic independence. Each presents a different kind of sacrifice, raising difficult questions about what we value and what we are willing to give up.

I remain hopeful about what AI could make possible, and deeply uneasy about the society we might build around it. I have no desire to surrender my belief in individual liberty, but I am beginning to question whether the economic arrangements I have long defended will remain capable of protecting it. Perhaps the real test of our convictions is whether we can recognize when the means we have chosen no longer serve the ends we value.

title: Secret agent bot: accessibility matters for the agents even if you can’t see them
text:
Secret agent bot: accessibility matters for the agents even if you can’t see them

The semantic structure screen readers have used for decades now also decide whether ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, and Perplexity can read your page at all.

In 2016 I had a series of calls with the federal government’s top accessibility expert as the leader of a design team, and I learned more in those conversations than in years of reading specifications. I had already been building accessible web applications since 2006, chasing Level AAA when most teams would not commit to AA. I learned so much, and it’s always been top of mind.

The lede even back then: accessibility matters, and we should pay attention to it.

For a long time that work served a small, often-overlooked audience you defended on principle alone.

That argument just changed just got larger.

Your website has a new kind of visitor, and it does not look at your page the way you do. It reads a stripped-down model of the page called the accessibility tree — the same structure browsers have built for screen readers for two decades. It doesn’t know what a color is; it looks for well-labeled structure.

If you don’t have it, it can’t find you. And most sites don’t have it.

The numbers: In early June 2026, Cloudflare reported that automated traffic had passed human traffic on the web for the first time, roughly 57 percent of page requests against 43 percent.

A fast-growing share of web traffic is agents acting for people.

The audience that reads through structure of your pages to understand context is no longer a rounding error, it is most of your traffic. Welcome to inclusive design. The questions narrow: which agents read what, when accessibility becomes load-bearing, and the small set of categories worth fixing first.

I’ll be covering all of the major agents on how they read a page in a later series of articles because it’s fascinating, but this is a good place to start.

How the Major Vendors Read a Page

There are three ways an agent can take in a page: it can look at a screenshot with a vision model, read the raw HTML of the document, or read the accessibility tree the browser builds from that HTML.

Each has a cost.

A screenshot is expensive in tokens and easy to misread when layouts are dense. Raw HTML is noisy, thousands of tokens of wrappers and scripts around the few elements that matter, frankly because of poor engineering practices and human slop code.

The accessibility tree is the cheap, clean option: a short list of the interactive elements, their roles, their names, and their states. Google’s own guidance for developers is that capable agents combine all three, leaning on the structured channels and using the picture to confirm layout. That’s pricey, and also means 3 different results.

The vendors split on where they start

  • Anthropic’s Computer Use is vision-first: Claude looks at screenshots and counts pixels to place the cursor, which is flexible but fragile when the screen shifts. Its browser extension, Claude in Chrome, leans the other way — its read_page tool takes the accessibility tree first, with a get_page_text tool for article-style pages and screenshots as the fallback.
  • Microsoft went the other way, at least for developers. Its Playwright MCP, the official server for letting a model drive a browser, works from structured accessibility snapshots and skips vision entirely, on the stated premise that the structured view beats a screenshot. Its consumer surface is the opposite: in Copilot Mode in Edge, Copilot Actions read and act inside your signed-in session, leaning on what is on screen.
  • Google’s Gemini agents sit in the hybrid middle. It blends the structured channels with a visual pass to confirm what the layout is doing rather than committing to one or the other. For users that shows up as Gemini in Chrome and its Auto Browse mode, with Project Mariner as the research agent behind it.
  • The most telling case is OpenAI. Its Computer-Using Agent, which drives both Operator and the Atlas browser, started from screenshots. OpenAI’s own publisher guidance now tells site owners that Atlas uses ARIA tags, the same labels and roles that support screen readers, to interpret page structure, and points them to standard accessibility practices. Even the company whose agent leads with pixels is telling you to fix your accessibility tree.

When Accessibility Becomes Foundational

Accessibility does not matter equally on every page, and it is worth being precise about where it does.

For a page that is mostly prose, an agent can usually cope; the words are the content, and even a messy structure leaves them readable. The stakes rise the moment the agent has to act — to find the right button, fill the correct field, choose among options, and move through a flow without losing its place.

Transactional, multi-step, and dynamic interfaces are where a broken structure stops being an inconvenience and starts being a brick wall.

If a keyboard user cannot finish the task, the agent usually cannot either.

The evidence is getting concrete. In the A11y-CUA study presented at CHI 2026, researchers at UC Berkeley and the University of Michigan ran Claude Sonnet 4.5 through 60 everyday web and desktop tasks under different conditions.

  • With normal access the agent finished about 78 percent of them.
  • Constrained to keyboard-only navigation — the path an accessibility-tree agent depends on — success fell to 42 percent, and the work took roughly twice as long.
  • Under a magnified viewport it dropped to 28 percent.

The same structural gaps that strand a screen-reader user strand the agent. If a keyboard user cannot finish the task, the agent usually cannot either. Accessible structure is not a separate track from agent-readiness; it is the track.

Legibility Is Not Endorsement

Building a page an agent can read is not the same as endorsing every agent that reads it. Anil Dash has argued that some of these products are openly hostile to the open web, substituting synthesized summaries for the pages and links underneath.

Legibility and approval are different things.

He is right that legibility and approval are different things. You can make your page structurally honest and still decide a given browser is a bad deal for the web, and hold the two judgments apart. The discipline stands on its own terms: it serves the people using assistive technology no matter what you make of any agent.

The Nielsen Norman Group makes the parallel case from the design side, treating agents as a class of user you now serve whether you meant to or not — which is a reason to build for them, not a verdict on them.

There is a sharper version of the cost, and it cuts against the grain of this whole piece. A page that is accessible and semantically correct is the easiest kind of page for an AI assistant to read, summarize, and answer from — which makes it the easiest kind to lift without sending anyone your way.

Do the structural work well and the assistant may cite you, paraphrase you, and keep the user inside its own answer.

It’s literally reverse SEO — honor the standards and pay the cost. Welcome to the world of AI.

The same legibility that wins the agent can cost you the click, and the ranking that used to come with it. That is a real tradeoff, not a reason to ship a broken page, but go in with your eyes open.

Where To Start

Category One: Semantic Structure and Landmarks

This is the foundation, and the cheapest win. Native HTML elements announce themselves in the accessibility tree without any extra work. A <button> is a button the agent can find and trust.

A <div> wired up with a click handler is an unnamed, role-less box the agent has to guess about, and it guesses wrong often enough to matter. The web.dev guidance is unglamorous on purpose: use the element that means what you intend, and most of the structure takes care of itself.

Two things sit on top of that foundation. Headings are the outline an agent reads to understand what a page contains and how its parts relate; a logical order, h1 to h2 to h3 without skipped levels, gives the agent a map instead of a pile.

Landmarks — navigation, main, header, footer — tell it which region it is standing in.

None of this is new advice. It is the same structure the field has taught for years, now with a second reader who takes it literally.

Category Two: Names, Roles, and States

Every control an agent might use needs a name in the tree, a role that says what it is, and — when it changes — a state that says what it is doing now. This is where most real pages fail. Icon-only buttons with no label, links that all read “read more,” custom dropdown menusand modals built from generic markup: each one lands in the accessibility tree as a blank or a question mark.

The agent can see that something is there and cannot tell what it does.

ARIA exists to fill the gaps native HTML cannot express — to give a custom widget the role and state it would otherwise lack. But it comes with a sharp rule the vendors tend to skip past.

The First Rule of ARIA is not to use ARIA: if a native element already carries the meaning, use it, because a wrong or empty ARIA attribute is worse than none.

It does not leave the tree blank; it fills the tree with confident, incorrect information, and the agent has no way to know it is being misled. OpenAI’s guidance tells publishers to reach for ARIA. Accessibility practitioners have pushed back that the durable fix is correct markup, not bolt-on attributes — and the data is on their side.

Here is the part that should bother you. In 2026, web accessibility got worse for the first time in six years. WebAIM’s annual scan of the top million home pages found detectable WCAG failures on 95.9 percent of them, up from 94.8 percent, with the average page carrying about 56 errors across 1,437 elements — a 22.5 percent jump in page complexity in a single year. ARIA usage climbed 27 percent, and the pages reaching hardest for it carried the most errors.

WebAIM names a likely culprit: AI-assisted coding. The same wave of agents now reading your page is helping generate the broken structure that makes it unreadable.

We’ll talk about that harness needed in a later article.

Category Three: Text Alternatives and Labels

This category is about the content that is real on the page but invisible in the structure unless you make it explicit. Images are the obvious case: without alternative text, an agent cannot tell a product photo from a logo from a chart, and a linked image with no alt text becomes a link to nowhere. WebAIM still finds missing alternative text among the most common failures on the web, year after year.

An agent cannot fill a field it cannot name.

Form fields are the same problem in a different place. An agent cannot fill a field it cannot name, so a label tied to its input is the difference between a completed checkout and an abandoned one.

The fix is dull and well understood: real alternative text on meaningful images, an empty alt on decorative ones, and a programmatic label on every input.

Category Four: Feedback and Stable Layout

The last category is about what happens after the agent acts. State has to be announced, not just shown. If a confirmation appears only as a visual change, the agent acts as if nothing happened.

If a confirmation appears only as a visual change, the agent acts as if nothing happened.

A result, an error, or a status update that never reaches the tree leaves the agent guessing; live regions and managed focus are how you tell it the page moved.

And layout has to hold still.

Agents that fall back to a screenshot lose their footing when the same control sits in a different place on every page, so consistency stops being a matter of polish and becomes a matter of whether the agent can find the thing at all.

The Work Is Already Specified and Has Been For Years

Here is the reassuring part, rare in a piece about new technology. You are not being asked to optimize for some proprietary new format. The thing agents need from your page is the thing the accessibility community has asked for all along: semantic markup, named controls, real text alternatives, honest state, stable layout.

That work used to pay once, for the people using assistive technology. Now it pays twice, because the same structure is what the machines read.

So treat it as triage, not a rebuild. Do not try to agent-proof every page. Find the flows where an agent has to act — the checkout, the booking, the account change — and make those legible first.

Open your browser’s developer tools, look at the accessibility tree for that flow, and ask whether you could finish the task from the tree alone. Then walk it with the keyboard only. Where you hit a wall, so does the agent.

The audience that reads through structure was easy to ignore when it was small. It is not small anymore. The web you can see is increasingly the smaller half of the room, and the other half is reading the tree you built — or the one you didn’t.

Here’s What to Consider

Before you change anything, weigh these:

  • Whether an agent would act on the page, not just read it. Static prose is low-stakes; the checkout, the booking, and the account change are where structure turns load-bearing.
  • Whether you could finish the key flow from the accessibility tree alone. Open your developer tools, look, and then walk the same flow with the keyboard only. Where you stall, the agent stalls.
  • Whether every control has a name, a role, and a state. Icon-only buttons and links that all read “read more” are the blanks that strand an agent.
  • Whether you are reaching for ARIA to patch markup that should be native. A wrong or empty attribute is worse than none, because it fills the tree with confident, incorrect information.
  • Whether images, fields, and feedback are spelled out. Alt text, tied labels, and announced state are what keep them from being invisible in the structure.
  • Whether the layout holds still across similar pages. An agent that falls back to a screenshot loses its place when the same control moves.
  • Whether legibility means endorsement. It does not — you can build an honest page and still judge a given agent a bad deal for the web.

title: Tesler’s Law: complexity moved to a different part of the journey
text:
Tesler’s Law: complexity moved to a different part of the journey

AI did not remove the complexity of software. It removed the interface that told you where the complexity went, and who is now paying for it.

Larry Tesler is the reason you can cut, copy, and paste. At Xerox PARC in the 1970s he and Tim Mott built Gypsy, the first editor where text stayed editable without entering a command mode first.

Steve Jobs recruited him to Apple in 1980, where he stayed 17 years and rose to chief scientist, driving a car whose license plate read NO MODES. He spent that career deleting the states that confused people, a UX career before the field had a name.

By the mid-1980s he had turned that instinct into the law of conservation of complexity, which says the hard part of any application cannot be removed, only handed to somebody (or something) else.

“Every application has an inherent amount of irreducible complexity. The only question is who will have to deal with it — the user, the developer, or the system.” — Larry Tesler

Forty years later the chat box arrived and looked like an answer: type what you want, the machine does the rest, no menus, no modes, no manual.

It was not an answer, it was a transfer, in three directions at once.

Some moved into the model, which is real progress. Some moved onto the user, who now writes the specification and judges the result. The rest went to your team, into evaluation work nobody staffed.

Tesler’s law did not get repealed. Moving difficulty is the job of design, so the transfer is not the failure. Concealing it is.

Eight points on where it went.

The Law Nobody Repealed

He names three parties where most UX writing collapses the question to user versus system. Here’s an example for today’s world:

The user

  • Then. Learned the menus, the modes, a shortcut or two.
  • Now. Writes the instructions and then reviews whatever comes back.

The application developer

  • Then. Conditional logic, 100 error strings, every edge case anyone caught.
  • Now. Evaluations, retrieval plumbing, and prompts that quietly became product logic.

The platform developer

  • Then. Microsoft or Apple, on a release cycle you could plan against.
  • Now. Your model provider, changing what it absorbs every few weeks without telling you.

This column is new, because a role appeared that Tesler had no reason to name.

The reviewer

  • Then. Nobody, since the person doing the work was the person checking it.
  • Now. Certifies output nobody in the room produced.

Four columns means a ledger, and this is how design has always worked. Every clean screen you admire was paid for out of one of those columns, and the screen never says which. Simplicity in an interface is almost always someone else’s workload.

Simplicity in an interface is almost always someone else’s workload.

The difference now is speed. The transfer moves more at once, and leaves no mark on the interface where it landed.

Count the Receiving Side

A ledger is good news, because it makes the whole thing countable. If a feature saved the user 10 minutes, those minutes showed up somewhere you can already instrument: review time per artifact, evaluation hours your team now spends, inference cost per task. Almost nobody counts them, which is why the savings look free.

Almost nobody counts them, which is why the savings look free.

That is a gap in practice rather than a limit of the technology. It closes the first quarter somebody measures both ends of a transfer.

Which leaves an answerable question nobody has asked out loud. Menus and modes were bounded, learnable, and the same on Tuesday as on Monday. Writing a specification and carrying the decision are neither.

We may have spent 40 years taking work off the user and three handing some of it back.

The Text Box Is a Transfer

Jakob Nielsen called generative AI the first new interaction model in 60 years, in AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years. Users state the result they want instead of the steps. He is right about the shift, but telling a system what you want requires knowing what you want, in detail, in words. That is a specification, and writing one used to be a professional skill with training and review.

It is now the control surface for hundreds of millions who never asked for the job.

Amelia Wattenberger named the cost early in Why Chatbots Are Not the Future. A text field looks identical to a search box, a login form, and a credit card field. Users can learn which prompts work, she wrote, but the burden sits with every user. A blank text field is the most flexible control ever shipped and the least instructive.

A blank text field is the most flexible control ever shipped and the least instructive.

A dropdown teaches you the domain while it constrains you. A disabled button shows a rule you would otherwise discover by failing.

Verification Is the Bill

In July 2025, METR ran a randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers across 246 tasks in repositories they had maintained for years. The result, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, was a 19 percent slowdown when AI was allowed. They forecast a 24 percent speedup going in and estimated 20 percent coming out.

Sit with that gap. The finding is not that the tools failed, it is that professionals could not feel where their own time went.

METR has since labeled those numbers historical, and redesigned a 2026 follow-up after too many developers declined to work without AI. Whatever the speedup is now, the tools are foundational.

Generating feels like progress in a way that verifying never will.

The work did not disappear. It changed from producing to checking, and checking is harder to see.

So design for the checking. Show a diff instead of a wall of replacement prose, and put the source where the decision gets made.

Where AI Absorbs Real Complexity

Here is the part the critique skips. Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond studied 5,172 customer support agents for Generative AI at Work in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025. AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by 15 percent, and less experienced workers improved in both speed and quality while the most experienced saw small declines.

That distribution is the finding.

The system absorbed complexity that took years of tacit knowledge: the phrasing that calms an angry customer, the judgment about which policy applies. For an expert who already carried it, nothing was left to take.

Geoffrey Litt made the wider argument in Malleable software in the age of LLMs. The barrier to end-user programming was never desire, it was turning a rough idea into code.

AI is the first tool in decades that raised the ceiling on how much complexity the system side can hold.

That is a change to the equation Tesler wrote and it is also the outcome he spent a career asking for.

The Deterministic Floor

Some complexity does not move at all.

Payroll is the clean case, where a paycheck is either correct or it is a legal problem, because withholding is a rule with a citation and an audit trail. Ninety-nine percent correct payroll is failed payroll. The same holds for authorization, tax filing, reconciliation, dosing, and safety interlocks.

Stanford RegLab tested the best case in Hallucination-Free?, published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies in 2025 on products as they stood in May 2024. The tools were retrieval-grounded and built for lawyers by LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters. They hallucinated on 17 to 33 percent of queries.

The floor has a second half, and enterprise software sits on it. An underwriter, a claims adjuster, a clinician: their work is hard because the domain is hard, and no interface reduces that.

AI can retrieve the rule and draft the letter, but it cannot own the decision, because owning it means being the person asked why a year later. That accountability is a ledger entry, not a rounding error. The model can hold the search, never the settlement.

The model can hold the search, never the settlement.

Let the model prepare the change, then let deterministic code execute it and a named person approve it. That boundary is knowable before a line of code exists.

The Jagged Edge

Above the floor the boundary is not knowable in advance, absorption is uneven, and the unevenness stays hidden. Stanford HAI’s 2026 AI Index puts generative AI in at least one business function at 70 percent of organizations, while agent deployment stays in the single digits.

Tesler named the reason decades earlier. In Tesler’s Theorem and other adages and coinages he gives his version of what others call the AI Effect: intelligence, he wrote, is “whatever machines haven’t done yet.” Whatever a machine absorbs stops counting, so the edge moves without anyone announcing it.

I catalogued the same edge by artifact in A UX Designer’s Field Guide to What Survives. Ask for a research readout before the research exists and you get 10 pages in 20 seconds, every quote invented.

The user’s new job is knowing where the capability ends, and nothing in the interface tells them.

The old interface at least failed out loud. A model answers everything in the same steady voice whether it knows or not, a defect rather than a limitation, because presentation closes it.

Mark Steyvers and colleagues measured the calibration gap in What large language models know and what people think they know, Nature Machine Intelligence, 2025. Longer explanations raised confidence without improving the answer; aligning them to internal confidence narrowed it.

Allocation Is a Design Decision

Eric Horvitz wrote the decision procedure 27 years ago. Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces, presented at CHI 1999, treats each automated action as a judgment call with three inputs:

  • How uncertain the system is about the goal
  • What a wrong guess costs
  • Whether the person can cancel directly

The second input sets the bar. When the price of being wrong is a corrected paycheck, the answer is never a generated one.

Saleema Amershi and 13 colleagues published Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction at CHI 2019, validated with 49 practitioners, and Horvitz is on that paper too. The first two guidelines are the ones teams skip: say what the system can do, and how well it does it. You are allocating complexity whether or not you write it down.

You are allocating complexity whether or not you write it down.

The default allocation is a blank box, a confident answer, no capability signal, no cheap way to verify. It is the cheapest option for the team building it, which is the trade Tesler spent his career arguing against.

Conclusion

Tesler was arguing about menus and modes, and the stakes were minutes. The stakes now are whether a person can tell a correct answer from a confident one, a heavier thing to hand someone through a rectangle.

His law holds up anyway. What changed is the size of the container on the system side, and that change is real. Models absorb translation, tacit knowledge, and boilerplate no interface could carry before, right up to the deterministic floor where they stop. Tesler would have taken that trade in a second.

What also changed is that the transfer stopped announcing itself. A cluttered toolbar declared its complexity, loudly and badly, but it told the truth about the cost. A blank prompt says nothing, and the burden arrives unposted.

Your job is the ledger. Decide, in writing, which of the four columns each piece of difficulty belongs in, then build the controls that hold that decision in place. Constraints that teach. Capability signals that admit where the ground drops away.

The complexity is still there, and it is still conserved. The only thing you choose is who pays for it, and you are making that choice every single sprint, named or not.

Action Items

None require a model change.

  • Post the ledger entry first. Name the column that absorbs the irreducible complexity, where reviewers will see it.
  • Instrument the receiving column. An unmeasured transfer is indistinguishable from an improvement.
  • Turn one text field into a control. Where users type the same instruction repeatedly, give it a selector. A constraint teaches while it limits.
  • Budget verification time, not generation time. Count the seconds spent checking, not just the seconds saved.
  • Design for the novice gain. The measured wins concentrate among less experienced users.
  • Draw both halves of the floor. Mark which outputs must be exact and which decisions need an owner. The first gets deterministic code, the second a named approver.
  • Give the jagged edge three treatments. A source chip for retrieval, a visible hedge for inference, a refusal out of domain.
  • Audit against guidelines one and two. Check whether a shipped feature states its limits anywhere a user would look. Most do not.

title: Are synthetic users (really) the future of UX research?
text:
Are synthetic users (really) the future of UX research?

Human-centered design demands a limited use of AI-generated personas, if at all

A big debate among UX researchers is whether to use synthetic users in their studies. There’s one group of researchers who consider it no less than an abomination, unethical to use an artificial persona to test a product that serves humans. The second group defends it as a helpful tool that makes user research more efficient.

Looking at it through a pragmatic lens, I understand both perspectives. UX teams may consider using synthetic users for low-level artifacts, the parts of a study you can reasonably simulate.

Still, the word synthetic already tells you what you’re working with. These users aren’t real. As researchers and designers, our goal is to build products that solve real people’s problems. We need human feedback.

What if synthetic users can help us solve those problems without losing touch with the humans we design for? How far do we let them take us?

The problem of overoptimistic LLMs

A major challenge for any UX researcher trying to create a synthetic user is trusting a system that seems to always give them the answer they want to hear.

LLMs are way too positive and tend to flatter the person prompting them. Many companies are using this “prompt-to-please” research to their advantage, knowing the risks it entails. It’s simply too convenient to have a system that generates test users who love your product and only give positive feedback.

This, of course, creates a false sense of satisfaction that’s by all means unrealistic.

A 2025 study showed how this overly positive tendency of LLMs has affected UX research. Its title is a participant’s verdict: “She was useful, but a bit too optimistic.”

To conduct this study, the researchers gave eight UX designers an interactive AI persona called Alice to work with across three activities: user research, ideation, and prototype evaluation. Alice was fast and helpful, but she agreed with almost everything. The study describes “a consistent tendency to agree uncritically with design proposals.”

For example, a designer asked Alice whether a two-hour session about organic farming in her restaurant would help her gain customers. “Yeah, that could be really effective,” she answered. No doubts or constraints.

The researchers saw the same across proposals: responses stayed positive while the real-world complexities (cost, user adoption, resources needed) went unquestioned. Senior designers described the conversations as “one-way” and “self-affirming,” noting that Alice never treated a single idea as infeasible.

Participants did find her useful for early exploration. This is the use case I’d recommend UX design and research teams test first. A synthetic user can work well as a first touchpoint, as it can give you a broad understanding of the problem space.

Always keep in mind that over-optimism is persistent. LLM’s will almost always try to please the person prompting. We must explicitly ask for critique to get anything close to honest feedback.

Speed in preliminary stages of UX Research is a plus

Putting the tendency toward over-optimism aside, synthetic users do have one clear advantage: getting things done faster (at least in the early stages of the user research process).

It’s not easy to find a positive side to AI-generated personas, given that most opinions and articles are negative and focus on their limitations. However, I found a report showing that UX researchers do see some advantages, including speeding up their work.

User Interviews surveyed 150 researchers in May 2026 for The State of Synthetic Users study. The researchers who use synthetic users summed up their value in one word: convenience. Or, as stated in the report, “the ability to gather rapid feedback without the logistical pains of recruiting participants.”

Recruiting is the bottleneck in almost every study I’ve seen. In particular, finding the right people and scheduling interviews with them. Using synthetic users doesn’t require this step, which is one of the reasons why 41% of the researchers surveyed treat them as a preliminary tool, right before human research begins.

The methods where they’re rated most useful were survey and screener design (46%), usability testing for directional signals (34%) and early-stage research (32%). Nobody is using synthetic users to make the final calls.

There’s another, rather unusual application of personas that flips this idea around. I shared an example of it in one of my first newsletter issues this year, after reading an article by UX Writer Chinwe Uzegbu.

In that piece, Uzegbu describes how she used classic UX personas to improve AI, instead of using AI to generate personas. Her team was writing training queries for AI agents without knowing who the users were, so she built research-backed personas, including neurodivergent users, people with low technical literacy, blue-collar workers, and non-native English speakers.

The result Uzegbu obtained was richer queries that captured how people talk to AI. If that practice becomes standard, our personas can end up shaping the models that later generate synthetic users. Better models mean better synthetic users. Whatever level of quality synthetic users reach, they’ll owe it to properly conducted UX research by humans first.

How feasible is it to use AI-generated personas for UX Research today?

Conducting UX research successfully using only synthetic users isn’t possible. The speed at which AI is being implemented in our work may make this take obsolete in a few years, but as of today, human-centered research is 100% necessary and delivers the best results. Human complexity (our tone, hesitation, facial expressions, body language, and behavior) is irreplaceable.

People have emotions, and every person is different from the next, even inside the same profession. Their cultural experiences and mental models are different. Put five doctors of the same specialty in the same study, and you’ll get five sets of feedback, because they’re five different people. A synthetic user, by contrast, is homogeneous.

I spoke with Eric Mahlstedt, Vice President, User Research & Insights at SAP, whose team had already run the test: they recreated several of our previous UX research studies with synthetic users, then compared the responses with what they’d heard from real human participants.

Mahlstedt found the synthetic users’ responses to be overly generic. They were plausible, flat regurgitations of anecdotes anyone could find online.

“It felt less like conducting research and more like a sophisticated internet search, presented in a way that creates the illusion of empathy,” he said. “There is no substitute for talking to the humans who will be affected by a decision, especially when it’s a high-impact or high-risk decision, which we dedicate our research capacity to.”

We both agreed that synthetic users may be valuable as a hypothesis-forming tool. If a team is starting from a blank slate, synthetic users could help inform an initial hypothesis or identify areas worth investigating. They can provide a jumping-off point for further research, but never give absolute or definitive results because they can’t replicate human experience.

Synthetic users should only be used to scale human UX research

So, are synthetic users really the future of user research? No. That’s my flat answer. To get real people to do real work, you need real feedback. And the word “synthetic” says it all: these are not real people.

Yes, synthetic users can be used to scale a study, but they can never be the only data point we rely on to build products that are going to be used by humans. That’s the ironic part: we’re designing products for humans, so getting the data only from non-humans simply doesn’t make sense.

My advice is to use synthetic users only to extend the scale of human UX research you’ve already done. They can be another tool in the research process, but when it comes to key product research that affects people, synthetic research cannot be the one source you rely on.

Arin Bhowmick (@arinbhowmick) is Chief Design Officer at SAP, based in San Francisco, California. The above article is personal and does not necessarily represent SAP’s positions, strategies or opinions.
